Fontenay
fawn-tuh-NAY
n. (Bernard's second foundation, 1118, the most complete surviving Cistercian abbey)
From Latin fontanetum, a place of springs; French fontaine, a spring.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Fontenay in Burgundy was founded in 1118 by Bernard of Clairvaux, his second foundation, and moved to its present site in the valley of springs in 1130. It is the most complete Cistercian abbey surviving anywhere: church, cloister, chapter house, monks' hall, dormitory, infirmary, bakery, dovecote and forge all stand, the forge being among the oldest industrial buildings in Europe. Dissolved at the Revolution and used as a paper mill through the nineteenth century, it was restored from 1906 and is on the UNESCO list. This dictionary records Fontenay because what survives there is a pattern, and a pattern is a thing Scripture takes seriously. The tabernacle was built to one shown rather than designed, “look that thou make them after their pattern, which was shewed thee in the mount” (Exo 25:40), and the point is repeated, “According to all that I shew thee, after the pattern of the tabernacle” (Exo 25:9). Hebrews says the earthly was a copy of something real, “See, saith he, that thou make all things according to the pattern shewed to thee in the mount” (Heb 8:5). A form of words is likewise to be held, “Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me” (2Ti 1:13).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a pattern as an original proposed for imitation; a model as a copy or representation on a small scale; a form as the shape or external appearance; a forge as a furnace where iron is wrought; and to imitate as to follow as a pattern.

expand to see more

PATTERN, n. An original or model proposed for imitation; the archetype; an exemplar; that which is to be copied or imitated.

MODEL, n. A pattern of something to be made; a copy; a representation of something on a small scale; a standard.

FORM, n. The shape or external appearance of a body; also, a model; a draught; a pattern; manner; established practice.

FORGE, n. A furnace in which iron or other metal is heated and hammered into form; also, the work-place of a smith.

IMITATE, v.t. To follow as a pattern, model or example; to copy or endeavor to copy in manners and deportment.

Key Scripture

Exo 25:40 — "And look that thou make them after their pattern, which was shewed thee in the mount."

Exo 25:9 — "According to all that I shew thee, after the pattern of the tabernacle, and the pattern of all the instruments thereof, even so shall ye make it."

Heb 8:5 — "Who serve unto the example and shadow of heavenly things, as Moses was admonished of God when he was about to make the tabernacle: for, See, saith he, that thou make all things according to the pattern shewed to thee in the mount."

2Ti 1:13 — "Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus."

Modern Corruption

Bernard's second foundation, 1118: the most complete Cistercian abbey standing, down to the forge, and a paper mill for a century before its restoration.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture repeatedly makes a pattern binding. Moses is not invited to design the tabernacle; he is shown one and told to match it, with the instruction given twice for emphasis, “look that thou make them after their pattern, which was shewed thee in the mount” (Exo 25:40), “after the pattern of the tabernacle, and the pattern of all the instruments thereof” (Exo 25:9).

The second thing is what a pattern implies about its original. Hebrews treats the whole tabernacle as a copy of a greater reality, which is why the exactness mattered, “See, saith he, that thou make all things according to the pattern shewed to thee in the mount” (Heb 8:5). Paul carries the same idea over to doctrine, where the words themselves have a shape that can be kept or lost, “Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me” (2Ti 1:13). Fontenay survives as the clearest surviving copy of the Cistercian plan; a dictionary is in the business of holding the form of words.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tabniyth (H8403), a pattern; Hebrew ra'ah (H7200), to see, to be shewn; Greek tupos (G5179), a pattern, a type; Greek hupotuposis (G5296), an outline, a form; Greek skia (G4639), a shadow.

expand to see more

Hebrew tabniyth (H8403) — a pattern, a structure shewn; “after their pattern, which was shewed thee in the mount”, Exodus 25:40.

Hebrew ra'ah (H7200) — to see; the pattern was shewn; “According to all that I shew thee”, Exodus 25:9.

Greek tupos (G5179) — a pattern, a stamped impression; “according to the pattern shewed to thee in the mount”, Hebrews 8:5.

Greek hupotuposis (G5296) — an outline, a form of words; “Hold fast the form of sound words”, 2 Timothy 1:13.

Greek hugiaino (G5198) — to be sound, healthy, of words; “which thou hast heard of me”, 2 Timothy 1:13.

Usage

"“after their pattern, which was shewed thee in the mount” (Exo 25:40) — shown, not designed."

"“according to the pattern shewed to thee in the mount” (Heb 8:5) — a copy of something real."

"“Hold fast the form of sound words” (2Ti 1:13) — doctrine has a shape that can be lost."
